title: Bill Owens and Wendy McMahon on Why They Left CBS News: ‘The Match Was Fixed’
full_text: Oct 9, 2026 8:10am PT Bill Owens and Wendy McMahon on Why They Left CBS News: ‘The Match Was Fixed’ By Ethan Shanfeld Plus Icon Ethan Shanfeld @ethanshanfeld Latest Bill Owens and Wendy McMahon on Why They Left CBS News: ‘The Match Was Fixed’ 31 minutes ago Robby Hoffman Sets New Netflix Special for 2027 1 hour ago Colin Jost, Danny Chun Set New Comedy Series ‘6 Bed 1 Bath,’ Produced Outside Studio System 20 hours ago See All Photos: Michael Bucker/Variety / Courtesy of Kseniya Berson Photography It was a CBS News reunion of sorts in Miami as former “ 60 Minutes ” boss Bill Owens and Wendy McMahon , the news division’s former president and CEO, detailed their 2025 resignations and spoke out against the current regime at the inaugural Jupiter Festival. “It was like the match was fixed, and I felt like I needed to do something to bring attention to it,” Owens said of his exit. “I was like a crazy person standing in the room with a grenade saying, ‘I’ll do it. I swear to God, if you take one more step.’” Related Stories A Rare David Bowie Self-Portrait — Featuring His Handprints — Is Going on Auction at Sotheby's ‘Bowie80’ to Celebrate David Bowie’s 80th Birthday With Events, Exhibits, Releases and More Throughout 2027 Owens left “60 Minutes” after nearly 37 years at CBS News, citing corporate editorial interference amid the network’s legal dispute with President Trump, who sued CBS and Paramount over the editing of a Kamala Harris interview. Seeking FCC approval for its sale to David Ellison’s Skydance, Paramount was preparing to appease Trump with a $16 million settlement, even as First Amendment experts argued the president’s lawsuit had little legal merit. Popular on Variety Leading up to the 2024 election, after “60 Minutes” ran an abridged promo clip of the Harris interview, Trump claimed the show edited his opponent’s remarks to make her appear more favorable. CBS rejected his claims and said the interview was not “deceitful” and “fairly represent[ed]” Harris’ answers. Owens explained that “60 Minutes” did not release the full transcripts of interviews because it would set a bad “legal precedent.” Still, top brass at the previous Paramount regime had other priorities. During this time, Owens said there was “interference” and “calls for editorial censorship” at “60 Minutes,” which came “from above, from ownership through corporate leadership.” “The corporation is telling us to do things that are not journalistically sound,” he said. “We’re pushing back against them. Now Trump is elected, and they don’t want us to be doing [negative] stories about [the new administration].” Owens said “60 Minutes” was doing the type of pieces the show has always done, investigating Elon Musk’s DOGE and mass firings at the Justice Department. But with more corporate eyeballs on the show ahead of the acquisition, Owens said, “Every week we’re being told, ‘Stop that. What are you doing?’” After Trump took office in 2025, FCC chairman Brendan Carr pressured CBS News to turn over the full, unedited transcript and camera feeds from the Harris interview, which were published on the FCC website. The result was underwhelming, as it became clear the interview had not been doctored but rather condensed, as is standard procedure for broadcast television. McMahon, who resigned less than a month after Owens with a vague statement about her disagreements about the future of CBS News, also elaborated on her departure: She didn’t agree with CBS’ apology and its settlement with Trump and she didn’t agree with the idea of the network having an ombudsman, which was later installed by the Ellison regime. McMahon said she departed because she looked at the direction the newsroom was heading and came to the conclusion that “I could not lead that from a journalistic perspective, or a business one.” Owens and McMahon resigned from CBS News in mid-2025, before the Skydance regime tapped Bari Weiss to serve as McMahon’s successor. The two echoed criticism of Weiss’ handling of the shake-up among the staff of “60 Minutes” this past summer. In August, reports circulated that Owens was looking to raise money for a new program, potentially even recruiting ex-“60 Minutes” correspondents like Scott Pelley to join. Sources close to Owens denied those reports at the time, and Owens did not divulge his future plans at Jupiter Festival. But he did talk about the Hollywood courting process that unfolded after he exited CBS News. “When I left ‘60 Minutes,’ all of the streamers wanted to talk to me and I had all the meetings,” Owens said. “Every meeting was the same. At the end they’re like, ‘Hey, we really appreciate what you did, et cetera, et cetera, but we could never work with you.’” The executive producer has a theory for why: “Because they had already paid their tribute to Trump.” Chuck Lorre Uses ‘Georgie & Mandy’ End Card to Troll Trump’s White House for Saying He Needs Psychiatric Help: ‘I Don’t Disagree’ Roseanne Barr Rages Against Ex Co-Star Michael Fishman for Saying ‘Roseanne’ Reboot Was ‘Rightfully Canceled’: ‘You F—ing Little Worm’ and ‘Brainwashed Bigot’ ‘Roseanne’ Star Michael Fishman Apologizes to Fans for the ‘Chaos’ of Roseanne Barr Feud: ‘I’m Gonna Keep Pushing Out Love’ Chuck Lorre Says Working on ‘Roseanne’ ‘Was Malice’ Because Roseanne Barr ‘Fundamentally Hated’ the Show’s Writers Loading comments...

title: Craig Ferguson & Megyn Price Starring In Addiction Dramedy Series ‘Quitters’ For Angel
full_text: Skip to main content By Andreas Wiseman Andreas Wiseman Executive Editor, Film & International @AndreasWiseman More Stories By Andreas Craig Ferguson & Megyn Price Starring In Addiction Dramedy Series ‘Quitters’ For Angel Faith & Family Outfit Ark Clb Launches With Former eOne Exec Venice Winner ‘A Day In The Life Of Jo: Chapter Phaedra’ Gets North American Deal With 1-2 Special View All October 9, 2026 8:08am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Craig Ferguson & Megyn Price Ian Cunningham/Courtesy EXCLUSIVE : Former late-night host Craig Ferguson ( The Late Late Show with Craig Ferguson ) and The Ranch and Rules Of Engagement star Megyn Price have been set to star in Quitters , a half-hour dramedy series whose eight-episode first season is now in production in Utah. The series will be distributed by Angel , the distributor-producer best known for its faith-leaning content. The synopsis reads: “After Liza (Price), an upbeat soccer mom, falls into the cycle of opioid addiction, she lands at Unplugged, an unconventional recovery center run by Nick McTavers (Ferguson), a former heavy-metal legend. To put her life back on track, Liza must learn to rely on an eclectic family of patients and counselors who help her navigate the long road of recovery.” Related Stories Acquisitions Angel Acquires Michael Keaton-Morgan Freeman Western 'Rode To Ruin', Launches Sales Arm Ahead Of TIFF Market News State Department To Screen 'Young Washington' At U.S. Embassies Producers are Eric Handler, Chase Vergari and Ibrahim Mohammed. It is being directed by Darrin “Fletch” Fletcher and Chet Thomas and produced through their FletChet Entertainment banner, which recently produced the Lionsgate title The Best Christmas Pageant Ever. Quitters was written and created by Dave Parkin. Watch on Deadline Executive producers on the series include Chet Thomas, Darrin Fletcher, Eric Handler, Chase Vergari, Ibrahim Mohammed, series writer and creator Dave Parkin, RoboCop and Starship Troopers writer Edward Neumeier, Rob Gibbs, HR Brown and Alema Harrington. Handler brought the package together and paired it with financing from Script 2 Screen Capital. Handler most recently served as executive producer on the Walton Goggins action-comedy Mister , the Samuel L. Jackson action film The Beast , and Maserati: The Brothers , starring Anthony Hopkins and Al Pacino. Vergari and Mohammed produce and finance through Script 2 Screen Capital, whose credits include By Any Means (Paramount Pictures), starring Mark Wahlberg, and Iconoclast , which premiered at the 2026 Tribeca Film Festival. “This is a world I have wanted to explore for as long as I can remember, and Nick McTavers is a character I understand in my bones. There is real truth in this story, and a lot of heart and humor too, and that is exactly the kind of thing I want to be making,” commented How To Train Your Dragon voice star Ferguson who has previously discussed his own addiction issues in his late 20s. “I’m so grateful for the opportunity to help tell Liza’s story. She’s funny and stubborn and heartbreakingly human, and her struggles through addiction and recovery are shared by so many people. My goal is to shed some light, hope and humor onto this issue, and remove the shame that acts as a barrier to asking for help,” added Megyn Price. “Ten years ago, HR and Alema, who have walked the road of addiction and recovery themselves, brought us this idea. Having Craig and Megyn lead the series now is the culmination of everything we’ve worked toward,” said Darrin Fletcher. Chet Thomas commented: “We want anyone struggling with addiction to know help is out there, and their families to understand what their loved ones are facing. We tell that story honestly but with the humor that so often keeps the people going through it alive.” “Nobody could play Nick McTavers the way Craig Ferguson does, and Megyn is going to break your heart and make you laugh in the same scene. I go back decades with Chet, from our DreamWorks days, and with Craig too, so having them both come together on a show that inspires hope means everything,” said producer Eric Handler. Angel’s slate of original series also includes the post-apocalyptic drama Homestead: The Series , now in its second season. Ferguson is represented by WME, Vault Entertainment, and Gang, Tyre. Price is represented by Independent Artist Group, Leslie Allan-Rice Management, and Myman Greenspan. title: Classic Moments With Dolly Parton, Remembered by the Actors Portraying Her in the Broadway Musical, ‘A True Original’: ‘I’m Jezebel, and God Loves Me Anyway!’
full_text: Oct 9, 2026 8:05am PT Classic Moments With Dolly Parton, Remembered by the Actors Portraying Her in the Broadway Musical, ‘A True Original’: ‘I’m Jezebel, and God Loves Me Anyway!’ By Jem Aswad Plus Icon Jem Aswad Executive Editor, Music jemaswad Latest Classic Moments With Dolly Parton, Remembered by the Actors Portraying Her in the Broadway Musical, ‘A True Original’: ‘I’m Jezebel, and God Loves Me Anyway!’ 35 minutes ago Gunna Launches SB the Label in Partnership With Atlantic Music Group 1 hour ago Clive Davis Pre-Grammy Gala Set for February 2027, a Tribute to the ‘Life and Legacy’ of Legendary Music Executive 24 hours ago See All For actors, portraying a real-life person is a huge challenge. But portraying a real-life singer-songwriter-actress-icon like Dolly Parton when she’s standing right in front of you is a whole other realm. That was the experience and the challenge for the actors and co-creators of “Dolly: A True Original Musical,” which previewed in Nashville last year and comes to Broadway’s St. James Theatre in previews starting on December 7, 2026, and opens officially on her 81st birthday, January 19, 2027. But while it was certainly a daunting task, it was a deeply enriching one for the people who have brought the musical to life. Related Stories ‘Bowie80’ to Celebrate David Bowie’s 80th Birthday With Events, Exhibits, Releases and More Throughout 2027 A Rare David Bowie Self-Portrait — Featuring His Handprints — Is Going on Auction at Sotheby's Parton was there for every step of the process, right up until her death from cancer this past August, and was every bit as positive, charming and encouraging as her iconic image would lead one to expect, according to two of the actresses who portray her — Carrie St. Louis (“Just in Time,” “Rock of Ages,” “Kinky Boots”) and Katie Rose Clarke (“Merrily We Roll Along,” “Light in the Piazza”) — and Tony-winning director Bartlett Sher and lead producer Adam Speers. All four sat down with Variety ’s Jem Aswad for an interview at Variety’s “Business of Broadway” event earlier this week. Popular on Variety Jem Aswad, Katie Rose Clarke, Bartlett Sher, Carrie St. Louis and Adam Speers speak onstage during the “Dolly: A True Original Musical” panel at Variety Business of Broadway presented by CNB held at Mandarin Oriental on October 05, 2026 in New York, New York. Kristina Bumphrey In vivid detail, they recalled their extraordinary and unique experiences with Parton as she helped them to shape her story and their depictions of her — complete with some of the most intimate and accurate Dolly impersonations the world is likely to hear. An edited transcript of this remarkable conversation appears below. The show, which examines Parton’s career in three eras, was written by Parton with Maria S. Schlatter, directed by Sher and executive-produced by Speers (who previously worked with Parton on the London incarnation of “9 to 5”) with Parton, her manager Danny Nozell, and Gavin Kalin Productions. It has been trimmed down from its three-hour-plus Nashville incarnation, but the version that is coming to Broadway was overseen and approved by Parton herself. Katie, Carrie, what sort of advice did Dolly give you? And have you ever had the experience of speaking with the person you’re portraying? St. Louis No, and certainly not at that level! I remember the first time I had to sing in front of her. Of course, it’s so nervewracking because you want to do her justice and honor her, but also it has to feel truthful and real and not like a caricature. The thing that was so beautiful about Dolly was, she made me feel so confident; she believed in me more than I believed in myself. I remember one day Katie and I mentioned that we still got nervous around her, and she said [in Dolly’s speaking voice], “Oh, don’t you start!,” you know? She would always kind of [gently slap] me and be like, “What are you talkin’ about? I’m just a normal girl!” And I said, “You’re right, my nana always says we all put our pants on one leg at a time.” And she looked right back at me and said, “Not me — I jump into mine with heels on!” (Laughter) She was just extraordinary. She was the first person in the building in the morning and the last person to leave. And on every break, you’d think she might go out and, I don’t know, attend to the 100 million other things that she was doing, but no: She would walk around the room and speak to every actor that was there, one-on-one. If people were playing the guitar, she’d start jamming and singing with them. She was just so normal and allowed us the room to explore and try things. She never said, “That’s not how I’d say that” — she would just say, “You make me look better than I am!,” which was not true. But she was just so wonderful and so confident in us. Clarke During one of my first rehearsals with her, we were on a break and Carrie and I had this really sweet moment where she shared some vulnerable things with us, and let her guard down. And when I was walking back into the rehearsal room with her, she grabbed my arm and put it through hers and was just kind of patting my hand. I said, “Dolly, I’m just never going to be over it. This is just wild to me.” And — same story — she goes, “Ooh, don’t you get it? I’m just a regular girl.” I felt like that was a clue to how to approach playing her, telling her story, and sharing her life on stage. I don’t think I ever really stopped being nervous to sing in front of her. Oh my gosh, “Jolene” — I have this huge hangup about singing “Jolene.” I would mess up the lyrics every time in rehearsals — “Sorry, Dolly!” [Imitates Dolly’s voice] “That’s okay, you’re doin’ great!” She was always harmonizing with us, Carrie and I would be singing with her around the piano and she would just sing along with us and she’d give us different harmonies to try. It was an unbelievable experience. We all keep saying to each other, thank God we had that summer with her. St. Louis What I think is really beautiful about our show is that you’re able to see the more private moments that the public maybe doesn’t know about. Because as bigger than life as she was, she was also pretty private, and she’s sharing a lot of these special, intimate details of her life — like her relationship with her husband, Carl, that were never seen in public. She would share these stories with Katie and me in the hallway, just talking about what he was like when they were dating and, how he courted her and things like that. She’s just a girl who was swept off her feet at the laundromat. It’s been really wonderful to be able to know that we’re telling her story honestly. How is the Broadway show different from the Nashville version? Speers We tried to put everything into the Nashville show: Dolly was 79 years old at the time, and she’d been in the spotlight for over 50 years, and I think one of the things we learned in our [Nashville iteration] was how much story there is. So [for Broadway], instead of telling the story of a global icon, what we really wanted to do was to tell a story of a human being. We expanded the areas that explained who she was as a human in order to dramatize that, rather than dramatizing the rags-to-riches [aspect]. It’s a story about how a human discovered who she wanted to be. Sher And she wrote over 10,000 songs, so there were a few to pick from. Our early workshops had over 50 songs in the show and would take three-and-a-half hours, so it was a huge amount of material to find our way through and hone in on the story that we have now. She was a big part of helping us to figure that out. Speers You still made her write another one! Sher Well, there’s a song early in the show called “Puppy Love,” which we have her singing at her radio debut at WIVK [in Knoxville, TN in 1956 at age 10]. That’s what we have in our show, but the song she actually sang at WIVK was “Little but Loud,” which was written by Little Jimmy Dickens, the famous Grand Ole Opry star. I said, “Dolly, why don’t we do ‘Little but Loud’? It’s such a great song and has so much information in it — ‘Little but loud, I’m poor but I’m proud,’” and all that sort of stuff. And we had a very intense, collaborative conversation about why she thought it should be a song that she had written. And then she went off and within two days wrote me a brand new song, which is now in the show, called “Mountain Girl” that is absolutely amazing. That’s what it was like working with her. She wrote a song every morning when she prayed. Did she record those songs or just remember them? Sher She had a whole system where she would take them to her team and they’d record them right there, or she’d call them up and say, “Meet me at the studio” and they’d go right in and record them. Speers She told me she did that so that every night when she went to bed, the world was a slightly different place for her being in it. Sher If you sat with her to watch the show, she always harmonized with [the actors] onstage — while you were sitting next to her, which I promise you is a pretty intense experience, to be sitting next to Dolly Parton while she’s singing along with herself. It was an incredible, incredible experience. St. Louis She was very, very involved. She was there every day in Nashville. Her dressing room was next to mine and Katie’s, so she’d come in at intermission and be like, “You’re doing real good out there, Dolly!” and I’d say “Thanks, Dolly!” Speers She’s all over this: She was my co-producer, she’s obviously responsible for the music and lyrics and she’s the co-author of the book. So she’s baked into this entire process, not just in what you see on stage, but also how we’re behaving off stage — we’re driven by how Dolly Parton wanted to treat everyone. What do you think were her priorities in telling her story? Speers I don’t want to speak for Dolly, but I can tell you what I think: It’s a story of hope, and I don’t think there is a more hopeful story out there than that of Dolly Parton, who came from absolutely nothing to become one of the most famous people in the entire world. So explaining how she did that, how she remained authentic, how she followed her heart to be a kind, generous, hardworking individual is the story we wanted to tell. Sher We talked with her endlessly about what the show was about. I did one of those old-school director things and sat down with her and said, “Dolly, if you were to put in one sentence what you think this show is about, what would it be?” And she said, “I’m Jezebel and God loves me anyway!” (Uproarious laughter) And that’s very much her. She embodied so many contradictions, so many parts of who we are. And that was a pretty good answer. Knowing how polite and diplomatic she was, how would she make her point if she didn’t agree? Clarke In the rehearsal room, whenever there was something we were trying to figure out or stumbling over, all of a sudden, from behind the table, she’d pipe up and say, “Well, what if we just did this and this? I don’t know…” And everybody would say, oh yeah, that’s absolutely right. And there were many times where we would start to do a scene and she would say, “Here’s what really happened,” and she’d tell us this whole story and we’d have “Storytime With Dolly” because she would be so willing to share every detail. I don’t know if some of these stories are public knowledge. So to be able to sort of sit at her feet and just listen to her life was an unbelievable gift. We would be around the piano and she’d start singing a line and I wouldn’t quite get the phrasing, and then she’d sing it a totally different way, and I would copy that, she’d change it up every time. She was like a collaborator. Katie and Carrie, what are the hardest songs to sing? Clarke Oh gosh. Well again, I had such a block with “Jolene,” but I think the hardest one to get through was “I Will Always Love You.” That was a really emotional one. On this one amazing day, we were just sitting around the piano, and she really met me where I was at and said, “You’re an actress. I want you to act it. Don’t be afraid to get it wrong.” And then she started singing it for me. And then, all of a sudden, before we know it, we’re all sitting there and she’s singing, “I Will Always Love You” with the piano, and the entire room was crying because it was just so beautiful. I have that recording on my phone — forever! And the more I am saturated with her music and thinking about who she was and who she is, the more in awe of her I am. What she modeled as a human being on earth — what a lesson for all of us. She’s just such a hero. I do find it to be difficult to get through “I Will Always Love You” without getting too emotional. St. Louis Wow. For me, it’s probably “Coat of Many Colors,” because in every interview she said it’s her favorite song she ever wrote. No pressure singing that for her! The message of that song is so simple but so beautiful and poignant because it’s about her own mother, and her relationship with her mother and feeling rich in love and not needing anything else. I remember the first day of our rehearsal for the Nashville run, I had a one-hour music rehearsal on the schedule. I said, “Okay, I know the music, I’m feeling ready.” But then Bart said, “So what we thought we’d do today is have Dolly sing all of your songs in the show, and then you’re going to sing them right after her.” And I thought [sarcastically], “Amazing! Can’t wait! That sounds like exactly what I want to do today!” (Laughter) So we went through the first couple of songs, and then we got to “Coat of Many Colors.” It was for me to learn her phrasing and kind of take in her version of it, but when she started, I stopped thinking about the phrasing and just realized that Dolly Parton, at 80 years old, is singing “Coat of Many Colors” to me by the piano. And I started sobbing, of course, because it was just so beautiful and she sounded perfect. She finished and looked up and said [Dolly voice], “Are you cryin’? You can’t be cryin’!,” and I was like, I’m sorry, this is the most beautiful thing that’s ever happened to me. But then Bart said, “Carrie, now you go.” So I just sang the song and trusted the material. I was told by a voice coach once to just serve the song, and that’s all you can do. So I did that — and I looked up and Dolly Parton was crying, and she said she was very touched by it. Yeah, it was maybe the greatest day of my life. And I’m honored to get to sing it every night. Speers I think Bart and I spent almost a week a month between [fall 2025] and June of this year, going down to Nashville and working with Dolly and her book co-writer Maria [Schlatter]. We’re really pleased that Dolly was a huge part of working out what we wanted the show to be post-Nashville [production] — what we learned from Nashville and how we were going to shape it for Broadway. The last conversation that Bart and I had with her, which was about 10 days before she passed, she was very open with us both: “You’ve got to keep going! This is the show that I want to be on Broadway!” Sher All of us have been so lucky to work on this with her in Nashville. But one crazy detail I always remember is that it’s the only time in my Broadway career where the person I’m working with is also on the license plates. (Laughter) Her picture is on the license plates for the state of Tennessee! It’s kind of a lot! And at the same time, how amazing and extraordinary she was. I think it’s a big lesson for all of us in this crazy country, which is such a mess, to see how someone can bring everybody together. It’s a very special thing. Jesse Whittock is here with you in the week Skydance took over Warner Bros. Discovery and Doctor Who began planning for the future. Here we go. Ready? ‘Doctor Who’ Regeneration Underway David Tennant in ‘Doctor Who’ BBC Studios Sonic screwdrivers at the ready: Stories about the Good Doctor with a question mark for a real name always do well on Deadline, and so it proved again with Jake and Max’s top scoop on the latest regeneration of the British sci-fi franchise. After the recent Russell T. Davies seasons were not brilliantly received by fans, Disney exited the show and rights owner BBC Studios (BBCS) put its future out to tender, asking the UK production community for their visions of a reimagined Doctor Who . One eye-catching bid in the “bake-off-style” process saw Line of Duty creator Jed Mercurio and his Hat Trick Mercurio indie throw its hat in the ring. Elsewhere, Line of Duty maker World Productions is down as is Criminal Record ‘s STV Studios, along with a pair of unnamed BBCS-owned labels , proving that while the show has become divisive and a difficult beast to tame, there will always be love for The Doc on British shores. Each producer sees a different future, with STV Studios’ plan being to move production north of the English border into Scotland for the first time in the franchise’s history. The deadline for pitches has now passed and our list isn’t exhaustive – another Scottish bid is rumored, for example. A24 UK, Playground, Mammoth Screen, New Pictures, Big Talk Studios, Expectation and Quay Street have, however, counted themselves out. The new series will premiere on BBC screens during the 2028/29 season, with the winner of the pitch selected in March. For the BBC, the news came in the same week that Director General Matt Brittin urged his staff to channel Elvis, i.e. “a little less conversation, a little more action.” Brittin wants the British public broadcaster to move faster, try more things and hone specialisms quicker. How it does that in a world of declining funding and ultra-competition isn’t clear. As some pretty snarky below-the-line comments on Jake’s scoop revealed, some aren’t convinced. “Be more Elvis, you mean, dead?” read one stinging post. Ouch. With Brittin also telling staff he’s been meeting U.S. streamers, it’s been another intriguing week at the BBC. title: $1.1 Billion for Five Warner Bros. Execs: Who Cashed Out From Paramount Sale
full_text: × Skip to main content By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All October 9, 2026 8:03am JB Perrette, the former CEO of global streaming and games for WBD, saw shares and in-the-money options net him about $157 million, while CEO David Zaslav cashed out $606 million David Jon/Getty Images The sale of Warner Bros. Discovery delivered a windfall for the C-suite of the company, filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission show. Former WBD CEO David Zaslav sold shares worth more than $224 million in WBD on conjunction with the acquisition by Paramount, while options that were in the money netted him an additional $381 million or so. That totals over $600 million, not including any cash severance, a tax benefit or other perquisites. But his top four deputies also sold their shares in the sale, netting more than $500 million between them. That includes former WBD CFO Gunnar Weidenfels and former chief revenue and strategy officer Bruce Campbell, as well as former international chief Gerhard Zeiler, who is now weighing a move to politics in his native Austria. It also includes JB Perrette, the former CEO of global streaming and games for WBD, who is the only member of the WBD C-suite to make the jump to Skydance where he is co-chair & chief business officer for TV and streaming. According to Form 4s that each of the executives filed with the SEC, Perrette’s shares and in-the-money options netted him about $157 million, with Campbell netting $129 million, Weidenfels netting $122 million, and Zeiler netting $92 million. Those are obviously subject to taxes and withholding, and the options are contingent on vesting. The payouts do not include any cash severance, transaction bonuses or other perks. Of course, the top five executives at WBD were not the only employees to own equity. Other top executives, including many who made the jump to Skydance, almost certainly held large equity stakes as well, and Zaslav made it a priority to get employees across the company invested in its success. About half of WBD employees held shares in the company. That means that there are likely other long-time employees who received generous, or at least modest, payouts. The New York Post’s Charlie Gasparino reported that around 500 employees will net at least $1 million, and 1,000 will net at least $500,000. But with Skydance set to drop the axe on many staffers in the coming months as they consolidate, it may not add up to much in the long run. THR

title: Edward Said’s Daughter Talks Israel-Palestine, Ed Sheeran and Why Bari Weiss Makes Her ‘Blood Boil’
full_text: Ulf Andersen / SantiagoFelipe.com “We’d always wanted something like this,” asserts Najla Said. Najla is the daughter and eldest child of the late scholar, intellectual and activist Edward Said , whose 1978 book “Orientalism” — examining the Western world’s skewed perception of the East — is considered a canonical work in the area of post-colonial studies. Born in Palestine and educated in America, Said taught comparative literature at Columbia University from 1963 to 2003, served on the Palestinian National Council and was the most prominent advocate in the U.S. for Palestinian human rights, urging the world to recognize the Nakba. Related Stories ‘Bowie80’ to Celebrate David Bowie’s 80th Birthday With Events, Exhibits, Releases and More Throughout 2027 A Rare David Bowie Self-Portrait — Featuring His Handprints — Is Going on Auction at Sotheby's Since his passing in 2003, Said’s work has only become more essential as the ethnic cleansing of Palestinians rose to the fore in the wake of the Oct. 7 attacks . Said’s life is chronicled in the new documentary “Edward Said: Between Worlds.” Directed by Maiken Baird (“Ghislaine Maxwell: Filthy Rich”) and produced by Alex Gibney ( “Musk” ), the film paints a loving portrait of Said as a Renaissance man — he was also a professional pianist who wrote four books on music — and tireless voice for Palestinian civil rights who was often met with contempt and mockery in debate halls and on the news. After playing the Toronto International Film Festival and New York Film Festival , the doc is currently seeking distribution. Popular on Variety Najla, an actress, playwright and activist in her own right, served as a consulting producer on the film, providing “a treasure trove” of archival footage, from home videos to photos, to aid the filmmaking team so they could “capture him as a whole.” Variety spoke with Najla Said about her father and their fight for Palestinians. Why did the timing finally seem right for a documentary on your father? When Maiken reached out just a few months after Oct. 7, 2023, we were really excited because it seemed like someone wanted to make a documentary that showed him as a whole person and wanted to use his words to tell the story. Because we were approached a few months after Oct. 7, it seemed like the timing was right to have these ideas reach a larger audience and not a niche crowd. What made the timing right after Oct. 7? What happened for many of us who are Arab American or Palestinian American is the time after Oct. 7 was difficult for us in a lot of ways. I felt overwhelmed because everything that was being discussed on the news and on podcasts was about this topic that my father had known so much about and done so much for. I started hearing people use his words and his arguments but had no idea where they came from. As more and more people are learning about the topic, I think it’s important to understand that Palestinians have been talking about this and writing about it articulately for decades. You get a sense from watching “Edward Said: Between Worlds” that your father was the lone voice for the Palestinian people on various talk shows and panels. That’s a heavy load to bear. What toll did it take on him? Growing up, you don’t really understand when your father does something unique like that. You just think, oh, that’s my dad. When I was about 12 or 13 the First Intifada started, he was really on television a lot and I began to understand and be really proud of him. What we all witnessed at the time was a lot of stress because it was dangerous. There were people threatening his life all the time, he had bodyguards around him, his office was firebombed and he would get really anxious because it felt like people were ganging up on him and he was the only person who was given voice to respond, so he had to carry it for everybody. You can see in the film that even his weight goes up and down, and TV presenters constantly condescend to him and say dehumanizing things to his face about Palestinians. At the end of his life, he decided not to do those TV interviews anymore because he didn’t think it was worth it. It takes a toll. How aware were you all that he was under FBI surveillance? I think he knew that. I used to talk to my best friend on the phone when I was in middle school and be like, “They’re listening!” I thought it was hilarious, but it was really terrifying when you think about it. I watched the movie “Munich” when I was older and realized I was probably in danger at certain points of my childhood that I didn’t know about, and that was sort of horrifying. Edward Said with his children Wadie and Najla in Jerusalem. Jigsaw Productions Your father says in the film, “The media has done a tremendous disserve to the cause of peace by misreporting the realities on the ground.” It’s part of an unaired portion of an ABC News interview where he’s discussing media coverage of Palestinians. How do you feel the media is treating the current moment? There are more people who can do what he did now and speak out, but very often they like to bring on someone who’s Jewish or Israeli who’s on the left instead of an actual Palestinian. You’re hearing more pro-Palestine voices in the media, but the actual coverage is unbelievably skewed and outrageous. During the Columbia University encampments two years ago, I had gone to the encampments and witnessed a bunch of people reading books, talking and eating, and then I went home and saw on the mainstream news a report where everything was absolutely skewed and a lie. It made me deeply upset. I was on campus teaching at the Columbia Journalism School during that time and what I found was that the media conflated what was happening outside the campus gates — which involved mostly non-Columbia students and/or outside agitators, since you needed school ID to enter campus — with what was happening inside the gates, which was mostly kids eating Dunkin’ Donuts in a circle. Right. It’s very jarring to see what is happening with your own eyes and then see something completely different on the news. I was really angry, and I felt that had [my father] been alive, it would have been different. I don’t know exactly what he would have done, but I just feel that. I could be holding on to the fact that the Columbia that my father worked at is not the one that exists now. During the time that my father got in trouble for throwing a stone, Columbia stood with him for academic freedom and they would never do that today. At the same time, his archive is in Columbia’s Butler Library and it’s one of the most visited places on campus. So, while they celebrate his legacy, they have also completely shat all over it, which is such an insult and so personally hurtful. The campus was our home and where we played as kids, so to have it be closed off and no longer be our home, and to have Gaza no longer be our home, felt very hostile and upsetting. Is a part of you glad he’s not around to see what’s happening over there right now? Yes. My mother has said that he would be so upset, so angry, so devastated that it’s better that he’s not here. However, were he here, I would feel more secure, guided and safe in the whole experience of being Palestinian during this time. I want to ask you about a graduate of the place where your father taught, Bari Weiss. She first made a name for herself trying to get Columbia University professors fired for criticizing Israel and speaking up about Palestinian human rights. Weiss is now running CBS News and is the right hand of David Ellison, who will also be controlling CNN soon. You just said Bari Weiss ’s name and I got hot inside. It infuriates me to know that these people get rewarded for their absolute, complete and professed racism. To be a “proud Zionist,” as she calls herself, and be able to be in control of a major news organization is so maddening to me. This is someone who tried to get professors like my father fired — as an undergrad! Some 19-year-old person came in and decided that an entire area of scholarship is racist and horrible and should be canceled, so for her to get all this power is very, very upsetting. I won’t even turn on the regular television anymore in case I see something from CBS News. I am really worried. I’m not sure if the average American knows this about her, but she is someone who makes my blood boil. Edward Said outside Columbia University circa 1968. Mariam Said How did you feel about the TikTok sale? Trump essentially pressured the company to sell most of its U.S. operation to a joint venture that includes Rupert Murdoch and Larry Ellison. The Council on American-Islamic Relations said,“ The main reason for the forced sale of TikTok to a consortium of pro-Israel billionaires is a desire to prevent young Americans from using the platform to learn about and oppose the Israeli government’s human rights abuses.” For sure . Because of my Palestinian-ness, I’ve been sucked into social media more than I otherwise would. I’m not on TikTok but I’ve seen plenty on TikTok over the last five years. With the younger generation, it almost feels like you’ve been bullied your whole life and now people are finally standing up for you. But now the Ellisons are going to own it and that is exactly why they bought it. That’s pretty terrifying because that has been the place where [the pro-Palestinian cause] has gotten the most movement in the past five years. It seemed as though pro-Palestinian sentiment picked up during the Black Lives Matter protests — that there was a sense of solidarity between those protesters and the pro-Palestinian movement. After Oct. 7 I lost a lot of friends — some were people I’ve known for my whole life, and I was like, I’m not sure who you thought I was, but I’ve always been Palestinian, so it seemed weird that they’d just stop speaking to me. But my Black and non-white friends are the ones who have not only been there for me but also are the ones who get it. I think that has a lot to do with the Black Lives Matter movement and what antiracism is, which you can apply to Zionism. That solidarity has been the most uplifting part for me because I would have nothing without it. You called out Shakira in 2011 for speaking at an Israeli conference, so I’m curious what your thoughts are on the whole Ed Sheeran-Macklemore dust-up over his saying “Free Palestine!” at a concert? I am very impressed with Macklemore , to be honest. He’s been pro-Palestine for the last few years and it’s not just words — he seems to really get it. I don’t know how Ed Sheeran would not have known [his stance] given all that Macklemore has done over the past three years, and the fact that he wrote a song called “Hind’s Hall.” I also think that because it was a conflation of so many things that are hot topics right now — billionaire oligarchs, free speech and Palestine — it all came together in this one, big thing where people could connect to it and there was a way in for everybody. Robert Kraft basically colluding with other stadium owners to keep someone out is a level of corruption that we often get upset with in this country, and it completely backfired. I never thought that if hip hop stood up for Palestine it would be a white dude from Seattle or wherever he’s from, but I’m glad that he did. What are your thoughts on Mamdani? His father is a professor at Columbia University like your dad. We’ve known their family for years, so I knew him as a little boy and my father knew him as a kid. I think he’s doing a great job. People get mad at me about that when he does things that upset Palestinians, but my theory is that he’s a Democratic politician working within the system, so I don’t know what people expect. I don’t expect him to be Che Guevara. I’m giving him more space to not be perfect than maybe other Palestinians do, and I believe in him as a human being. I think he’s a really good human being at heart. His mother Mira and father Mahmood are close family friends, and I do remember my father on the phone with Mira asking about Zohran when he was a little kid. He thought he was a cute little kid. He’s always been very thoughtful and very charming. The only time Benjamin Netanyahu’s name is invoked in the documentary is the time he backed out of a debate with your father while accusing him of being a “terrorist” and “antisemitic.” It happened twice. It happened on a TV show where he didn’t want to be in the same building as my dad, and then they were on a plane together and both seated in first class across the aisle from one another and Benjamin Netanyahu asked the stewardess to move him. My father then asked the stewardess why he moved, and the stewardess told my father, “He said you wanted to kill him.” Edward Said speaking with Palestinian children while filming BBC documentary “In Search of Palestine” in 1997. Charles Bruce “Edward Said: Between Worlds” doesn’t currently have a distributor, and we’ve seen other pro-Palestinian films like “No Other Land” and “NAZA” have to self-distribute. There seems to be plenty of public interest in this topic yet these films can’t get distribution. I am an actor by profession and have been in this world a long time, so I’m not surprised by it, but I am upset by it. One of the only ways that we can reach a mass audience and tell affecting stories is through film. I am hopeful that this film will get distribution, and I think it has a good chance because it’s a documentary that’s all archival footage. There is stuff in it that people will want to censor, but I don’t know if it will have the same level of outrage as “NAZA” or “No Other Land” because it’s not exactly about what’s happening now — it’s about this person’s life — but I know it’s been hard getting funding for it and getting people onboard. Your father believed that a one-state solution with equal rights for all is the best way to go when it comes to Israelis and Palestinians. People ask, “Do you think he would still think that given what has happened in the last few years?” I think that he would, as hard as it is. We’re not going to find a way out of it by isolating Palestinians and Israelis from each other. That’s just not going to happen. The only feasible solution is equal rights for all people, end of story, so I don’t think he would have given up on that. He’d see that it was much more difficult now, but I think he would still hang on to it. What do you hope people walk away with after seeing “Edward Said: Between Worlds?” I think people — and young people, especially — have done a great job of educating themselves on what happened in 1917, 1948 and all that, but I think — and my father says this — what is needed now is an acknowledgment that this happened to us. Through this film, you get to see the history of it. There are straightforward video clips of Israeli leaders stating their intentions very clearly; and you get to see, through my grandfather’s Super 8 films, a Palestinian society that was lost and how we got here. Not to sound too much like my father’s daughter, but there is something important in delving in deeper and understanding more in order to fight and move forward with this struggle. I’m also happy for them to get to know my father as a person, because he was very funny and charming. Loading comments... title: Troye Sivan Is at His Best on ‘She’s the Best,’ a Weird, Wild Exploration of Desire: Album Review
full_text: Oct 9, 2026 8:00am PT Troye Sivan Is at His Best on ‘She’s the Best,’ a Weird, Wild Exploration of Desire: Album Review By Steven J. Horowitz Plus Icon Steven J. Horowitz Senior Music Writer speriod Latest Troye Sivan Is at His Best on ‘She’s the Best,’ a Weird, Wild Exploration of Desire: Album Review 43 minutes ago Katseye’s Sophia to Resume Group Activities in January 2027: ‘I Can’t Wait to Share the Stage With My Sisters Again’ 23 hours ago Aerosmith Returns With Two Concerts at the Hollywood Bowl — Two Years After Announcing Retirement From Touring 2 days ago See All Ahead of his third album, 2023’s “Something to Give Each Other,” Troye Sivan teased the era as a dance-pop fantasia with singles “Rush” and “Got Me Started.” It was his post-pandemic record, one that promised to capture the crackle of electricity that came with no longer being on lockdown, finally free to connect with others. But those songs threw off the scent, as Sivan spent just as much time embracing the dancefloor’s escapism as he did sifting through the emotional wreckage of a relationship. What he ended up with was a varied body of work, a mature step forward for an artist who was still figuring out his sound and self as one of the leading gay male artists in pop. Related Stories ‘Bowie80’ to Celebrate David Bowie’s 80th Birthday With Events, Exhibits, Releases and More Throughout 2027 A Rare David Bowie Self-Portrait — Featuring His Handprints — Is Going on Auction at Sotheby's Sivan could have easily gone full party on his fourth album “She’s the Best” — one of its lead singles, the aptly titled “Party,” would suggest as much — but he instead uses the project as a canvas to look inward while testing the pliability of pop convention. Across the dozen tracks, Sivan leans heavily on ’90s touchstones, traipsing from glitch-hop to drum and bass, casting a wide net across sounds and scope. It’s a wild ride of an album that goes to many, many places, but what “She’s the Best” lacks in uniformity, it makes up for in ambition, favoring aesthetic over immediacy in what ends up being Sivan’s best, albeit weirdest, album to date. Popular on Variety At 31, Sivan has been famous for more than half of his life, first as a young YouTuber broadcasting from his native Australia and subsequently as a pop star making sense of his sexuality in the public eye. His trajectory has yielded canonically queer singles (“Bloom,” “My My My!”) that, perhaps backhandedly, have always suggested he’s just one hit single away from unlocking the next level of pop stardom. It’s a path he could have easily continued to take with “She’s the Best,” yet here he forgoes the easy route in favor of songs that invite closer listening, revealing layers of emotion and melancholy beneath the veneer of synths and the chug of guitars. Sivan dedicates the album to the women around him, the ones who radiate strength as much as they do cool. He enlists a long coterie of producers and songwriters to bring his vision to life, including Jack Antonoff, George Daniel, Finneas, Tayla Parx, and his longtime collaborator Leland, who co-writes every track. As always, he’s wont to have a good time, like on the deadpanned “Party,” or the UK garage-powered “Troye Meets World” with the thesis “music meet body, body meet music.” But “She’s the Best” is more concerned with lust and desire, about longing for permanence in an unstable world. There’s an interiority to the album that Sivan’s previous records merely gestured towards, on songs like the plucky “Cowboy,” where he croons about a man that came to him in a dream, or twinkling “Embarrassingly,” an admittance that he pleasures himself to the thought of a former lover. He’s quick to surrender to carnal desire, but regularly pines for more. “Find hot singles in the Los Angeles area,” he sings on “I Do This For You.” “Sorry for descending into some type of hysteria, I’m just a little lonely.” These are deeply personal admissions on a pop album of this caliber, yet Sivan makes these confessionals feel plainspoken. (Sometimes, maybe a bit too plainspoken, at least to any naive listener who comes across a track like “Canada Dry,” written as a “slinky back arch pop” song about a Canadian he wants to… engage with .) That’s likely because Sivan often sings in italics, not bold, allowing his voice to add to the production without overpowering it. He isn’t the most gifted singer — just ask him, he’ll agree — yet he’s learned to wield his voice as its own instrument, holding the focus at just the right time and letting go when the production takes focus. On “FF,” for instance, he slinks across a languid breakbeat on the verses — “Grab the neck of your guitar in a way that makes me jealous, better play it for me,” he sings — before slipping into an Auto-Tune falsetto on the chorus, his voice getting carried away in a wash of instruments. To that end, Sivan is as much a performer as he is a curator of his own vision. He cares more about tone and storytelling, as he’s said, and prioritizes accordingly. It’s to his benefit: “She’s the Best” is a snapshot of a mainstream artist unafraid to pivot off the conventions that come with it so long as it plays to his own strengths. Sivan has been doing this for over a decade, yet he’s never sounded so sure of what kind of artist he is, even when he sings of his own uncertainty. Very few artists are capable of holding those truths simultaneously, yet Sivan does it with ease, the keeper of the keys to his own kingdom. title: Geeta Gandbhir, Sam Pollard, Alisa Payne Board ICE-Themed Oscar Contender ‘Water Cooler’ As EPs
full_text: Skip to main content By Matthew Carey Matthew Carey Documentary Editor, Awards @mattcarey More Stories By Matthew IDFA Announces Forum Lineup: Projects From Wang Bing, Rachael Leah Jones, Vitaly Mansky, Juanjo Pereira, Liang Zhao & More Lightdox Acquires Sales Rights To ‘Nostalgia For The Future,’ Documentary On Enigmatic Filmmaker Chris Marker Narrated By Charlotte Rampling ‘Ash And Crayons’ Trailer: In Evgeny Afineevsky’s Film, Wounded Ukrainian Children Show Will To Survive And Thrive View All October 9, 2026 8:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source A masked ICE agent in 'Water Cooler' Spoonbill Stories/Message Pictures EXCLUSIVE: Academy Award nominees Geeta Gandbhir , Sam Pollard , and Alisa Payne are joining the Oscar-contending short documentary Water Cooler as executive producers. Emma V.F. directed the film, which she shot in the corridors of immigration court at Federal Plaza in New York City. Filming openly, V.F. captured scenes of jarring contrast: ICE agents engaged in mundane “water cooler” talk and then those same agents seizing migrants in the hallways who were following proper procedures to seek legal status in the U.S. At one moment, the agents – most of them masked – would be talking amongst themselves about shopping for Black Friday deals, for instance, or the latest taser models. The next moment, they were forcibly detaining someone who had showed up to immigration court little expecting to be grabbed before they walked into court. Related Stories News London Film Festival: Sam Pollard To Lead Official Competition Jury News Sports & News/Doc Emmys Set 2026 Lifetime Achievement Award Recipients; 'Have I Got News For You' Trio To Host Ceremonies A masked ICE agent in ‘Water Cooler’ Spoonbill Stories/Message Pictures “The observational documentary — which [V.F.] filmed from November 2025 through January 2026 — juxtaposes agents’ casual conversations with tense scenes of the agents arresting immigrants who attended required court hearings to seek legal status,” notes a description. Water Cooler won Best Documentary Short at Palm Springs International ShortFest 2026, qualifying the film for Oscar consideration. “ Water Cooler is an urgent documentary short that sends a powerful message about a defining issue of our time,” said Pollard ( MLK/FBI , Tutu ). “America is at a tipping point with ICE and their outrageous incursions into our cities, which is why films like this are so important.” Gandbhir ( The Perfect Neighbor , The Devil Is Busy ), observed, “Emma V.F.’s film Water Cooler honors the direct cinema style pioneered by Bob Drew and D. A. Pennebaker while turning her lens on masked federal agents. Even in a short runtime, it does what the films of those pioneers did — immerses you in a world that is crucial to see for yourself.” Masked ICE agents confer in ‘Water Cooler’ Spoonbill Stories/Message Pictures Water Cooler screens on Saturday at the Hamptons International Film Festival in New York, on Sunday, October 18 at the Woodstock Film Festival in New York, and on October 24 at AFI Fest in Los Angeles. Next month, it’s programmed at the St. Louis International Film Festival. In addition to Palm Springs International ShortFest, the documentary has screened at DC/DOX in the nation’s capital. The documentary is a production of Spoonbill Stories and Message Pictures , the latter a company founded by Gandbhir, Pollard, and Payne (Payne earned an Oscar nomination earlier this year for producing The Perfect Neighbor ). Water Cooler is directed, produced, filmed and edited by Emma V.F. Along with Gandbhir, Pollard, and Payne, Blair Foster ( Marty, Life is Short ; Taxi to the Darkside ) serves as an executive producer. Robert Aiki Aubrey Lowe ( Seeds , Union , Power ) composed the original score. V.F. directed the 2023 documentary feature Queen of New York . Her producing credits include In the Same Breath (HBO); Silver Dollar Road (Amazon Studios); Take Your Pills: Xanax (Netflix) and Once Upon a Time in Uganda . “As the granddaughter of Italian immigrants and Jewish New Yorkers who would be outraged to see masked federal agents disappearing law-abiding people down stairwells in their city, I knew this was a film I needed to make,” Emma V.F. said in a statement. “I’m thrilled to partner with Message Pictures to share the film more widely in hopes that it inspires collective action opposing ICE.” Watch a teaser-trailer for Water Cooler here: Netflix Eyes Major Layoffs; Would Be First Big Staff Reduction Since 2022 Int’l Boss Gerhard Zeiler Exits; Zaslav Cashes In; TCM To Film Group; Latest Skydance UK Network 5’s Profits Slump Amid Streaming Investment HBO Orders ‘Crazy Rich Asians’ Series From Adele Lim, Jon M. title: Sarah Snook & ‘Game Of Thrones’ Stars Shows Adapted As Microdramas For Snips
full_text: Skip to main content By Jesse Whittock Jesse Whittock International TV Co-Editor @WhittockTweets More Stories By Jesse Sarah Snook & ‘Game Of Thrones’ Stars Shows Adapted As Microdramas For Snips ASOB Media Offers MIPCOM Buyers ‘A Study On Beauty’ Icelandic Drama ‘Elma’ Set For Siminn Bow As Glassriver Debuts ‘NCU’ At MIPCOM View All October 9, 2026 8:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Snips Snips EXCLUSIVE: Succession star Sarah Snook and Game of Thrones actors Maisie Williams , Liam Cunningham, Iain Glen and Kit Harington are making their microdrama debuts. Vertical video platform Snips is adapting series that each actor or actress has starred in for the new medium, as the platform continues to seek films and TV shows to repurpose in 9:16 ratio. The show are Australian drama The Beautiful Lie , an ABC series starring Snook; Sky dark comedy Two Weeks to Live , starring Williams and Sian Clifford ( Ludwig ); Rome drama Domina , starring Cunningham; BBC drama Prisoners’ Wives , starring Glen, and BBC and HBO co-production Gunpowder , starring Harrington. Related Stories News PBS Masterpiece's 'Maigret' Finds UK Home News Alternativa Distribution Takes 'No Good Men' & 'Four Daughters' To MIPCOM Each show will be transformed from its full-length format into 45-second to two-minute episodes. Watch on Deadline The Beautiful Lie debuted on ABC in Australia in 2017 as a modern reimagining of Tolstoy’s Anna Karenina , with Snook (known best as Succession ‘s Shiv Roy) playing a retired tennis champion married to another tennis legend, who flies home to help her brother’s crumbling marriage, only to meet and feel an instant attraction to a charismatic music producer – who happens to be the brother of her sister-in-law. Two Weeks to Live debuted on Sky in the UK in 2020, and follows Williams as a young woman on a secret mission to avenge her father’s mysterious death when she was a child, who along with her mother joins a pair of socially awkward brothers and goes on the run from murderous gangsters and the police. It was Williams’ first lead role after her run as Arya Stark in GOT . Domina , another Sky show, debuted in 2021, when Cunningham playing the father of young Livia Drusilla (Kasia Smutniak), whose lose of her family sets her on a path to seizing power in Rome. Isabella Rossellini and Claire Forlani joined Cunningham, who played Ser Davos Seaworth in GOT . Glen stars in Prisoners’ Wives , a two-season BBC drama from the early 2010s. The show follows the wives, girlfriends and partners of prisoners, with Glen playing a career criminal whose lavish lifestyle is running out, along with his money. Polly Walker ( Rome ); another GOT star, David Bradley; and a yyoung Phoebe Dyvenor ( Bridgerton ) also had roles in an ensemble cast. Gunpowder , a miniseries from 2017, was set in 1603 with Harington playing Robert Catesby, a charismatic Catholic nobleman, who decides to blow up the Houses of Parliament with the King inside. Harington who starred as Jon Snow in GOT , is a real-life descendant of Catesby, and lead a cast also including Liv Tyler ( The Lord of the Rings ), Mark Gatiss ( Sherlock ) and Peter Mullan ( My Name is Joe ). Snips model Snips has sought to set itself apart from other microdrama apps by focusing on repurposing existing shows and films for the vertical space, rather than making its own originals. “Viewing habits are changing, and people’s preferences are changing with them,” said Or Ben Shimon, co-founder and CEO of Snips. “That shift is exactly why the micro-drama industry has exploded the way it has. Now we’re seeing big-name actors get into the space, and that tells you everything about where this format is headed. We believe good shows are like music — they just need to be on the most modern format.” Snips has been offering rights owners a revenue-share model that allows earnings to grow based on performance over the more traditional flat license fee agreement. Shimon believes this gives actors a direct stake in their titles’ performance, incentivizing them to promote the work to fans and followers. Shimon is set to hit MIPCOM Cannes next week, meeting with sellers and content owners to acquire more titles for adaptation. title: Netflix Gearing Up to Lay Off 5% of Workforce: Report
full_text: Oct 9, 2026 7:52am PT Netflix Gearing Up to Lay Off 5% of Workforce: Report By Todd Spangler Plus Icon Todd Spangler NY Digital Editor xpangler Latest Netflix Gearing Up to Lay Off 5% of Workforce: Report 1 hour ago David Zaslav Gets $606 Million Payout From Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger 19 hours ago Kevin MacLellan, Paramount’s Head of Global Content Distribution and International, Is Leaving Skydance Post-Merger 23 hours ago See All Courtesy of Netflix Netflix is planning a major round of layoffs coming as soon as next week that would cut about 5% of its headcount, according to a new report. The streaming giant plans a significant restructuring that “will impact” about 5% of staffers and “could be announced as early as next week,” according to a report by Puck News, citing anonymous sources. A Netflix spokesperson declined to comment. It’s not clear which departments would be most heavily affected by the reported cuts. Popular on Variety Related Stories ‘Bowie80’ to Celebrate David Bowie’s 80th Birthday With Events, Exhibits, Releases and More Throughout 2027 A Rare David Bowie Self-Portrait — Featuring His Handprints — Is Going on Auction at Sotheby's As of the end of 2025, Netflix said it had about 16,000 full-time employees, which means a 5% reduction in force would eliminate around 800 jobs. Roughly 68% of its workers, about 10,900, were located in the U.S. and Canada as of December. The last major Netflix layoffs came in 2022, when it axed about 450 staffers following the streamer’s net decline of 200,000 subscribers in the first quarter of that year, its first such drop in more than a decade. The company has made additional smaller cutbacks since then, including letting go several dozen members of its global product team earlier in 2026. Ted Sarandos, Netflix’s co-CEO, at last month’s Bloomberg Screentime conference in L.A., said the company is growing — noting that in Q2, it posted double-digit revenue gains in every geographical region — but that “We want to keep growing it faster.” “Yes, overall, we’re not growing as fast as I want us to, and we’re working on making that move faster,” Sarandos said, addressing the slowdown in Netflix user engagement (which was up 2% year-over-year in the first half in 2026). He added that the streamer is “also doing things that create a lot of headwind to that number. Meaning, when we do live programming on Netflix, which is a relatively new thing, we spend about 5% of our content budget on live events. They generate about 1% of our watching.” For the second quarter, Netflix posted earnings in line with Wall Street forecasts but issued Q3 revenue guidance below analyst expectations, driving the stock price down. Netflix is scheduled to report third quarter 2026 earnings on Tuesday, Oct. 20, after market close. Related Stories News ASOB Media Offers MIPCOM Buyers 'A Study On Beauty' News Robby Hoffman Sets Second Netflix Special “I’ve spent much of my career sitting between filmmakers and studios, and I’ve seen extraordinary stories struggle not because the audience wasn’t there, but because the infrastructure and advocacy weren’t,” Maurice said. “Ark is about changing that. Created and written by two-time Creative Arts Emmy winner Gabbi Pascua and directed by Alan Dennis ( Morningside 5 , 30 for 30 ), A Study on Beauty explores culture, history, and human identity through the lens of beauty and wellness over seven episodes. You can see a trailer above. ASOB is framing it as “evoking the visual rigor of Chef’s Table and the cultural depth of Anthony Bourdain’s Parts Unknown – with intimate human storytelling.” We first told you about the doc in December 2024, when it was known as A Study on Beauty: Through Smoke . Related Stories News Icelandic Drama 'Elma' Set For Siminn Bow As Glassriver Debuts 'NCU' At MIPCOM Acquisitions Reelz To Follow The CW's 'Police 24/7'; Sky Remains On The Case For Season 3 Season 1 spans three distinct global chapters, with the first chapter, ‘Through Smoke,’ which charts art and heritage of French perfumery was filmed on location across France, including in Grasse – the world’s perfume capital located just up the French Riviera from Cannes, along with Spain, Monaco, Switzerland and Italy. There are also chapters on ‘Onsen,’ which look at Japan’s ancient hot spring bathing rituals and generational healing practices, and ‘Homeland,’ which head to the Philippines to look into matriarchal heritage, colonial history, and indigenous traditions with 109-year-old Kalinga tattoo artist Whang-Od, beauty pioneer Dr. Vicki Belo, ‘the first Asian supermodel’ Anna Bayle and Miss Universe contestants. title: TV’s Newest Scream Queen Summer H. Howell Has Been Preparing for ‘Carrie’ Her Whole Life
full_text: Skip to main content Howell tackles a new take on the iconic Stephen King character in Mike Flanagan's Prime Video adaptation of the novel. Photograph by JONNY MARLOW Logo text For someone on the precipice of a life-changing moment, Carrie star Summer H. Howell is surprisingly calm. The 22-year-old actress has spent the last year warming up to the idea that she was moving into a new phase of her career with the role as the titular character in Mike Flanagan ‘s Stephen King adaptation. Described as a new take on the iconic horror story, Carrie ‘s a natural progression, as she puts it, in the trajectory her career’s been on. Howell took her first role in a horror film at the age of 8 and hasn’t looked back since. “I feel like I’ve been preparing to be Carrie my whole life,” she tells The Hollywood Reporter on a recent Zoom. The show marks her first time leading a television project — or really any major television project. Related Stories TV Karen Read Series Starring and Executive Produced by Elizabeth Banks Ordered at Amazon TV Sam Bankman-Fried Docuseries Set at Amazon (Exclusive) But the show, which premiered on the streamer Wednesday, is exactly what Howell was looking for after gaining years of experience in horror films. “I kind of drew this whole project towards me,” she says. “I’m big into manifesting, and I write things like I have them already.” With this manifestation, it was less about the show itself and more about the environment — she later admits she actually didn’t know much about Carrie going in. She’d seen an image or a GIF here and there, but once she started auditioning, she stayed away from Carrie , both the book and the 1976 film, entirely. It was clear that Flanagan’s version was going for a different take on the story, so it just made sense. No need to worry, she’s since consumed both. Instead, Howell manifested working with “good, genuine people who are kind and want to make real art.” She realized once she was on set that her manifestations had been describing the crew of Carrie perfectly. Howell’s blind faith likely helped, but she also put in hours upon hours to grab the coveted role. She sent in her first tape for the project in January 2025. A month or so later, she sent in the next, new scenes and everything. And so it went for quite some time. While many young actors might’ve found nerves in a lengthy casting process, Howell found herself having a “really good feeling” about her situation. “I started getting deja vu, like I was on the right timeline or something,” she says. “I was telling my friends and family something’s going to happen; they’re going to want to talk to me. And they did.” The actress did a “long work session” with the casting team on a Friday in March 2025. Flanagan wasn’t on the call, something that, at the time, she was grateful for. She needed to focus. She did four intense scenes, including one where she’d have to cry. Finding some boldness within herself, maybe as only an actor with over a decade of experience can, she told the team: “If you want to see tears, it’ll happen on the day.” The call ended, and Howell was told Flanagan would watch over the weekend. “He didn’t,” she explains. “He watched it right away. All of a sudden I was back on a call.” Her manager called her with the request to redo the monologue, this time with tears. “I remember laying on my floor in my room just telling myself all these affirmations and how I’ve come so far,” she says. She did it and went into her weekend anxiously awaiting news. By that next Tuesday, April Fool’s Day of all days, Flanagan, backed with approval from King himself, called to tell her the good news. “The first thing my mom said to me when I got the part was, ‘Your life is going to change forever,'” she recalls. “I feel like I made it happen,” Howell says. “It was meant to be.” Below, the Carrie star speaks with THR about leading the project, why the show gave her hope as a young actor and what a typical day in her life looks like. What was it like for you to be number one on the call sheet and lead this project? That feels like a responsibility. If I hadn’t been acting before I got this job, I would’ve been freaking out the entire time. They probably would’ve fired me because I would not have made the space what I did with all my experience. That was one of the things Mike and I talked about on the first call, [that] he expected me to lead people, lead the actors. Me and Sam[antha Sloyan] were seen as the heads of the department in that way. But it came easier because of my experience. If I was complaining during prom [about] being covered in blood, nobody would’ve had a good time. Howell as Carrie White in Flanagan’s Prime Video adaptation. Courtesy of Prime Having worked in horror since you were very young, were you totally prepared for that day you had to spend prom covered in blood? I mean, you say day, but it was nine days. It might’ve been 11, if we’re including after prom. I was prepared, but I didn’t understand until I was there and I was doing it. A lot of patience required, relying on other people to touch everything for me. I couldn’t really do much because my hands, down to the fingertips, were covered and [they’d tell me] “Don’t mess up the continuity!” When you are stepping into the role of Carrie and you have Mike Flanagan at the helm, are you just trusting that he’s going to lead you in the right direction? What does that partnership look like? Absolutely. I mean, it took time to build that trust, but it came very quickly. It was apparent from the start that Mike… Once you’re chosen by Mike, you’re in this little family. As long as you’re nice to people and you do your job — you show up ready — that’s all he asks of us. He told me right from the start, as much Carrie is his and Stephen’s, she’s now mine, which is unbelievable to think about. He trusted us. I mean, he knows he’s a man and that this is a woman’s story. He made a point to hire women who could shape it the way it needed to be told. We had a lot of powerful directors and powerful women behind the scenes helping us out. It’s just so nice to be given that space and listened to. Did that give you a little bit of hope as a young actress in this industry? Oh, absolutely. You never know who you’re going to have to work with going in, so it was so reassuring knowing Mike is so kind and prioritizes our comfort and our safety. He makes sure we’re happy with the people we’re working with. There were no mean people. We all got along so well, and Mike was pleasantly surprised with that. He kind of paved the way. It gives you hope for sure. Was going back and forth between school and acting something you found difficult as a child? Maybe a little bit. I was the only actor growing up, so I was known for that, and people view me a certain way, I’m sure. It’s made me think back on things. Maybe they saw me a certain way and that’s why we weren’t friends, for whatever reason. It’s strange, for sure. Being a child actor can be very sketchy and weird, but as long as you’re good people… I was very lucky. My mom has always looked out for me and been my rock and stood up to whoever she needed to and taught me how to do that myself. It was awkward sometimes, but… Sloyan, Howell and Flanagan attend Prime Video’s “PROMiere” celebration of Carrie in New York City. Jamie McCarthy/Getty Images for Prime Video What’s something about you that you think people would be surprised to know? The first thing that comes to mind is that I’m 22. When I’m not dolled up, I look very young. It’s funny, I checked into the hotel the other night, and we went down to the lounge. The guy told us to come back at a certain time for the champagne thing. “Not for you, but for you,” [he said] to my mom. I was like, well, I’m 22, but OK. What does your ideal day off look like? Make some good food. I like to cook, so I’ll make something. Spend time outside. Preferably, it’d be nice out and not the middle of winter in Manitoba, which can be awful. Spend time with my loved ones, curl up on the couch, watch some TV with my mom, hug my dogs all day and block out the world. What are you hoping to do next? Are you looking outside of horror? I like to branch out. Not in a leave horror behind way. I still love horror, and I will continue to do horror but it’d be nice to go to work and not cry and scream all the time. I just filmed an action movie called Runaway , so that’ll be coming out sometime next year. I really enjoyed that. Besides all the bruises I walked away with, it was really worth it and fun. I’d like to do some action-adventure or a dramedy or get myself into comedy, maybe. I’d like to do it all. THR

full_text: Oct 9, 2026 7:44am PT Phoebe Bridgers Reunites Boygenius as Part of Three-Song Studio Performance Video, Directed by ‘Primetime’ Helmer Lance Oppenheim By Chris Willman Plus Icon Chris Willman Senior Music Writer and Chief Music Critic ChrisWillman Latest Phoebe Bridgers Reunites Boygenius as Part of Three-Song Studio Performance Video, Directed by ‘Primetime’ Helmer Lance Oppenheim 1 hour ago Steve Martin and Alison Brown on Reinventing Lil Nas X’s ‘Old Town Road’ as an All-Star Bluegrass Tune… With Added Lyrics About Buc-ee’s and Sasquatch 23 hours ago Hayley Williams Proves There’s a Lot More to Her Than Paramore in a Galvanizing Solo Show at the Hollywood Bowl: Concert Review 2 days ago See All Phoebe Bridgers fans may not be getting glimpses of her current arena tour, because of the prohibition on cameras and phones, but as far as performance footage goes, she’s given them something better — a three-song in-studio video, shot by her “ Primetime ” director Lance Oppenheim , that features some familiar guests. The filmed performance, part of the “Sound Check at Cherry Lane Theatre” series, has Bridgers singing the closing theme she wrote for “Primetime,” “On Video,” followed by two choice picks from her “Lost Weekend” album, “Haunted” and “Lost Boys.” She’s joined for the last two numbers by Julien Baker and Lucy Dacus , amounting to a Boygenius reunion. The two women also sang harmonies on those two songs on Bridgers’ album, but this acoustic performance provides a much more intimate listen to their vocal interplay. It’s the first time Bridgers, Baker and Dacus have appeared together on camera in nearly three years, specifically since they did “Saturday Night Live” as a group in November 2023. Bridgers and company shot this new footage with Oppenheim following her three sold-out nights at Barclays Center in Brooklyn. The location, Cherry Lane Theatre, is a venerable off-Broadway theater — said to be New York’s oldest — that is now owned and operated by A24, which put out “Primetime,” in which Bridgers has a supporting role, as well as having provided a theme. “On Video” is the first of the three songs in the video, with Bridgers performing in dim lighting in front of a bank of televisions, accompanied only by Jay Gruska, one of the co-producers of the latest album, on keyboards. For “Haunted,” a much jauntier-sounding number with a pronounced country flavor, Bridgers is joined by Dacus, who wields a video camera of her own, and Baker, plus four acoustic musicians. The lineup gets stripped down to just the Boygenius trio for the finale, “Lost Boys,” which has a much softer arrangement than the spirited acoustic version, emphasizing the group harmonies. Bridgers fans will well know that this is Oppenheim’s second time filming a version of “Lost Boys.” He also directed the official music video for the lead single from “Lost Weekend,” with some visual and thematic callbacks to his three-part 2024 HBO documentary, “Ren Faire.” Popular on Variety Related Stories ‘Bowie80’ to Celebrate David Bowie’s 80th Birthday With Events, Exhibits, Releases and More Throughout 2027 A Rare David Bowie Self-Portrait — Featuring His Handprints — Is Going on Auction at Sotheby's Oppenheim is also the co-director of the much-touted upcoming Elizabeth Holmes documentary, “You Can See Everything,” with Nathan Fielder. “Primetime” marks his debut directing a dramatic feature film, dramatizing a story about TV personality Chris Hansen; Bridgers appears in it as a “decoy” attracting potential sexual predators. The “Sound Check at Cherry Lane” installments can be seen on A24’s YouTube channel. Past such performances were provided by artists including Tame Impala and Blood Orange.
