title: Dawn Porter to Direct Documentary on Pioneering TV News Anchor Max Robinson
full_text: Oct 9, 2026 7:32am PT Dawn Porter to Direct Documentary on Pioneering TV News Anchor Max Robinson By Cynthia Littleton Plus Icon Cynthia Littleton Business Editor @Variety_Cynthia Latest Dawn Porter to Direct Documentary on Pioneering TV News Anchor Max Robinson 1 hour ago Let’s Get Physical: Key Takeaways From The IRL Advantage, Variety’s Experience and Culture Summit 21 hours ago Fox Entertainment Global Keys on Content Creators, Microdramas With Diverse Mipcom Slate 1 day ago See All Variety / ©ABC/Courtesy Everett Collection Dawn Porter is set to direct a feature documentary on pioneering Black TV news anchor Max Robinson for Wise Child Studios . CNN anchor Victor Blackwell is among the producers. “Color Bars: The Story of the Black Journalist Who Broke the TV News Color Barrier” will recount the rise and fall of Robinson’s career in broadcast news for Wise Child Studios. Porter, known for her much-praised docus including 2020’s “John Lewis: Good Trouble” and 2018’s “Bobby Kennedy for President,’ will produce through her Trilogy Films banner. Blackwell, who anchors “CNN This Morning Weekend” and hosts the weekly series “First of All with Victor Blackwell,” will produce through is Fresh Fruit Films. Related Stories ‘Bowie80’ to Celebrate David Bowie’s 80th Birthday With Events, Exhibits, Releases and More Throughout 2027 A Rare David Bowie Self-Portrait — Featuring His Handprints — Is Going on Auction at Sotheby's “Max Robinson was an exceptional journalist by any standard, and he deserves to have a firm place in the history of American journalism,” said Jason Beekman, founder and CEO of Wise Child Studios. “He courageously broke barriers in front of a national TV audience while facing the incredible pressure of simply doing his job. We’re proud to bring his life and legacy to a wider audience, and thrilled to have Dawn Porter’s vision guiding the film.” Popular on Variety Robinson came on to the national scene in the late 1970s as an anchor for ABC News. He gained prominence as an anchor for the NBC and CBS affiliate stations in Washington, D.C. In 1978, Robinson made history by joining ABC News’ national anchor team. He was a founder of the National Association of Black Journalists in 1975. But Robinson’s tenure at ABC News was short-lived as he struggled with alcohol abuse. He died of complications from AIDS in December 1988 at age 49. Robinson is an inspiring figure to a generation of journalists and media business insiders. “I remember watching Max Robinson on television — he was one of the very few Black people on the evening news,” Porter said. “Later I joined ABC News and people still spoke about his impact on the newsroom. At a time when truth and courage in journalism are under assault, everyone should know the Max Robinson story.” Blackwell equated Robinson’s impact to that of Sidney Poitier, Thurgood Marshall and Jackie Robinson. “Max Robinson is my Sidney Poitier. He’s my Thurgood Marshall, my Jackie Robinson,” Blackwell said. “In our current media landscape and social climate, Max’s life and career are more relevant than ever. I’m excited and honored that Dawn has joined the team to tell his remarkable story.” Wise Child Studios was formed in 2023 to develop and package a range of original content. Beekman is a former head of business and legal affairs for RadicalMedia. Wise Child’s investigative docuseries “Reality Check: Inside America’s Next Top Model” debuted on Netflix earlier this year. title: Robby Hoffman Snags Stand-Up Sequel at Netflix
full_text: × Skip to main content By Chris Gardner Plus Icon Chris Gardner chrissgardner Follow Sign Up View All October 9, 2026 7:30am Robby Hoffman attends the Vanity Fair Oscar party hosted by Mark Guiducci at Los Angeles County Museum of Art on March 15, 2026. (Photo by Amy Sussman/Getty Images for Vanity Fair) Robby Hoffman is back in the Netflix fold. The Emmy nominated performer, who debuted her first stand-up special on the streamer in December 2025, has struck a deal to return to Netflix with a follow-up. A new one-hour special is set to debut globally on Netflix in 2027. Production company Rotten Science will be producing the outing. No other details have been revealed, like where or when the special will be recorded. As mentioned, it follows the first one, Robby Hoffman: Wake Up, which covered topics like her unique upbringing as part of a large, ex-Hasidic Jewish family, political correctness, gender identity and pronouns, wealth, Hollywood success and more. Also a lot of venting : “It’s a way of going to the gym for me. For me to complain is to enjoy, to understand. It’s a catharsis. If I’m yelling at you, I’m thrilled. I’m happy to be talking to you.” Related Stories Movies 'Animals' Review: Ben Affleck Directs and Stars Opposite Kerry Washington in a Thriller Full of Juicy Elements That Should Be a Lot Tastier Movies 'Cyberpunk 2077' Live Action Film in Development at Paramount Pictures The special had a Hollywood heavyweight behind the camera, too, as it was directed by stand-up superstar John Mulaney . During his Netflix is a Joke appearance with David Letterman earlier this year, Mulaney gushed about Hoffman, calling her a “total original,” and likening her debut to the late and great Sam Kinison, “someone who you’re, like, ‘I’ve never heard of a comedian like this. I’ve never seen anyone this unafraid.'” He added: “When she opened for me in San Diego at an outdoor venue on the water with lots of couples at tables, she never adjusted her act for anyone.” Hoffman works as a writer, actor and comedian. She had a role on the last two seasons of HBO’s Hacks , and earned an Emmy nomination for outstanding guest actress in a comedy series for her work on it. She is currently in the HBO series Rooster opposite Steve Carell, and her credits also include a role opposite Michelle Williams in FX’s critically acclaimed Dying for Sex . Hoffman is developing her own starring vehicle, UnEntitled . THR

title: ‘The French Connection’: THR’s 1971 Review
full_text: × Skip to main content By Craig Fisher Plus Icon Craig Fisher View All October 9, 2026 5:58am 1971's 'The French Connection’ Everett On Oct. 9, 1971, 20th-Fox unveiled William Friedkin’s The French Connection in theaters. The Gene Hackman thriller went on to land 8 nominations at the 44th Academy Awards, claiming five wins including for best actor, director, writing, editing and picture. The Hollywood Reporter’s original review, headlined “Fox’s ‘French Connection is a first-rate thriller,” is below: The French Connection has already been open for three weeks in New York, where it is reported to be doing land-office business. It’s easy to see why. The picture is a first-rate thriller about the investigation and crackdown of a heroin-smuggling operation, set mostly in New York, and scripted by Ernest Tidyman from the Robin Moore book. And the director, William Friedkin, knew what he was about. Almost from the beginning, you can feel your stomach muscles tightening because you’re afraid of missing something, and as the movie goes along, you can sense the audience sliding forward in their seats, straining to catch every detail. It’s an astonishingly well-edited film, with a spectacular chase sequence in which Marcel Bozzuffi, the screen’s newest man-you-love-to-hate (he was the homosexual murderer in Z ), is in an elevated train with his pistol at the conductor’s head while Gene Hackman, as a police detective, chases him by car from below, careening at top speed around pedestrians and track supports and other cars. (Philip D’Antoni, the producer, also produced Bullitt .) And it’s filled with sharp, funny bits of business in the action and dialogue: Bozzuffi tearing a piece of bread from a loaf clutched by a man he’s just shot in the face; Fernando Rey, the mastermind behind the connection, fishing in the bay behind his home in Marseilles; the inflection that Hackman gives to the word “cute.” The film is most impressive, however, for the fact that Friedkin, after The Birthday Party and The Boys in the Band and the predominately backstage The Night They Raided Minsky ‘s, has finally gotten outdoors not simply for surface dazzle, as in Minsky’s , but to give depth and texture to his story. In recent years, New York has become such a familiar location in American movies that I think it’s safe to say that, even for non-New Yorkers, the New York back grounds lately have hardly been notice able. But Friedkin and his cinematographer, Owen Roizman, have suc ceeded in integrating the action and the backgrounds, often wittily, as in a sequence when Bozzuffi and Rey dine in high style while outside the restaurant, staking them out, Hackman gnaws on a limp slab of pizza. The score by Don Ellis is shrewdly and sparely used, and the movie is uniformly well-acted, by a cast that also includes Roy Scheider, Tony LoBianco, and Harold Gary. The character of Det. “Popeye” Doyle is less The French Connection ‘s protagonist than its chief participant, and so Gene Hackman is still denied a true star role; but Hackman is rousingly good in it. Hackman, who was so fine as Clyde’s brother in Bonnie and Clyde and as the ski coach in Downhill Racer and as the son in I Never Sang for My Father , has quietly be come one of the most memorable actors in our movies. Now if they could only find a leading lady for him. — Craig Fisher, originally published on Oct. 29, 1971. The Hollywood Reporter ‘s original review of The French Connection .
